title: I wanted to see how far AI coding tools have actually come, so I took an older prototype and turned it into a working multiplayer ARPG. Zero assets, everything generated in code by AI.
author: idlerunner00
selftext:
I ran a version of this experiment about a year ago. It was fine. Mostly frustrating, some good moments, nothing I kept. I wanted to try again with the current generation of tools and find out where the ceiling is now.
    
    So I dug out an old prototype of mine, moved it from PixiJS to Three.js, and made it properly multiplayer. Authoritative server on a fixed tick, area-of-interest interest management, binary protocol over WebSocket, client-side prediction and reconciliation.
    
    I used Claude Code and Codex, and I gave myself one hard constraint: 
    **zero assets.**
     No sprites, no textures, no models, no audio files. Every visual is geometry, particles and shaders built at runtime. Every sound is synthesized from oscillators. Partly because I can't draw, mostly because I wanted to know whether code-only content actually works and I did not want to play around with spritesheets or models again.
    
    **What the game is**
    
    An ARPG extraction runner. There's a persistent hub where you sort your loot and your build, and from there you drop into endless runs. A storm chases you from behind, so standing still is not an option. You go deeper, you get better drops, and every checkpoint asks the same question: bank what you have and leave, or push one layer further. Character power comes from collectible specialist souls with upgradeable skills rather than fixed classes.
    
    
    **What worked well**
    
    Domain-Driven Design, seriously. I named the domain explicitly before writing much of anything. Hub, Run, Storm, Checkpoint, Soulstone, Run-Stone, Affix. Once that vocabulary lives in the code, you and the model are talking about the same things, and a one-line instruction lands where you meant it. This did more for output quality than any prompt trick I tried. 
    
    Golden rules, checked in every phase. This is the one I'd hand to anyone starting something like this. I wrote a short list of non-negotiable rules up front, and every task gets checked against them at every stage, not just at review. A few of mine:
    
    - A rule (damage formula, item roll, stat derivation) exists in exactly one place and is used by both the server and the client. If you feel the urge to copy logic, you extract it instead.
    - No art assets. Ever. If it can't be generated in code, it doesn't ship.
    - New content (a monster, an affix, a skill, a run type) is data in a registry. Adding content must never require touching engine code.
    - Assume hundreds of concurrent players from day one. The client is never trusted. No design decision may assume single player.
    - Every upgrade counts and has visual impact. A +1 on a skill rank has to visibly change how the cast renders. No two ranks look alike. This includes every upgrade in the game. 
    - Do it right immediately. Never ship a shortcut you'd have to undo, even if the clean fix touches ten more files.
    
    Coherence across a large codebase was the thing I expected to lose. The rules are the reason I didn't (fully). They also settle arguments instantly, which matters more than it sounds I think.
    
    *Build one standard, then build on it.*
     One well-named component per concern, reused everywhere, never a second implementation of something that already exists.
    
    *The PixiJS to Three.js move was almost boring.*
     I had budgeted real pain for this and it turned out to be the easy part of the whole project. It took about 24 hrs for a full port, was reallly impressed by this.
    
    *Dev tools are effectively free now.*
     This is the thing I will keep telling people about. I have a map painter and generator, a pile of test setups and harnesses, and a short clip creator for recording footage. None of these would have existed if I'd had to hand-write them, because none of them were worth the time. Now they do not even cost an afternoon each.
    
    **What didn't work as well**
    
    Characters. Pets came out great (I think). Creatures came out okay and I'm mostly happy with them, some of them are properly funny. Player characters I fought with and I'm still not satisfied. Not sure if I will fully get there if I spend more time on them. If someone has a workflow for this without it involving assets, please share!
    
    **Compared to a year ago**
    
    It isn't an incremental improvement, it's a different activity. Last year I spent my time correcting output. This year I spend it deciding what should exist. That's the whole difference, and it's a much better job. I am kind of shocked to see how much has changed in only a year and are already wondering how it will be in 2027 around this time.
    
    **If you want to look at it**
    
    I've put the prototype online at **idlerunner.com** for anyone who wants a look. Browser, free, no download, guest login. I'll leave it up for a few hours today and then take it offline again.
    
    Happy to answer anything about the architecture or the workflow in the comments.
    
    Link: https://idlerunner.com/

replies.author: idlerunner00
replies.body:
By prompting AI over and over. And obviously by including "make no mistakes" in every prompt.

Jokes aside: write down a concept and a set of golden rules first, then let the AI set up the workspace (git, docker, vite, typescript) and derive a domain-driven split into server / client / shared.

Here that came out as TypeScript end to end: Three.js + Vite on the client, Node server, plain `ws` with a binary protocol, Postgres. No engine, no editor, no assets.

* `shared` — pure game rules, nothing else. Damage formulas, item rolls, stat derivation, the wire protocol. Zero dependencies, no I/O, no rendering. Runs in Node and in the browser.
* `server` — owns the world. Fixed tick loop, authoritative.
* `client` — rendering, input, netcode.

Both import `shared`, so the damage formula exists once: the client predicts what will happen, the server decides what did, and they can't drift apart because it's literally the same function.

Then pick one piece and go deep. The terrain wasn't one-shotted, but a prompt like the one in my reply below is roughly where I'd start.

    Build a procedural, cartoon-styled 3D terrain renderer in TypeScript with Three.js.
    No textures, no image files, no models, no shader includes from disk. Every vertex
    position and every colour is computed in code at runtime.
    
    Read this whole brief before writing anything. Then build it in the stages at the
    bottom, and stop where I tell you to stop.
    
    ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    WHY IT IS SHAPED THIS WAY
    
    The single most important decision is that the thing which produces geometry is a
    pure function that has never heard of Three.js. Everything good downstream falls out
    of that: it can run in a worker, it can be unit tested in milliseconds without a GPU,
    and two different call sites can be proven to produce byte-identical output. If you
    let THREE.Vector3 leak into the compiler you lose all three, and you will not get
    them back later without a rewrite.
    
    ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    COORDINATES AND UNITS
    
    - Y is up. The grid lies in X/Z. Cell size 1.0, one elevation level = 0.5 in Y.
      Pick these constants once, export them, never inline them anywhere.
    - Elevation is an INTEGER level, not a float height. The terracing is the art
      direction, and it makes every geometry decision discrete, comparable and testable.
      "Is there a cliff here" becomes an integer comparison instead of an epsilon check.
    
    ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    STAGE 1 — THE MODEL (pure data, zero imports)
    
    A grid of cells. Each cell:
      level:    integer elevation
      type:     Floor | Wall | Water | Chasm | Bridge
      material: an id into a material table (grass, rock, sand, ...)
    
    The material table holds linear-RGB colour triples, not hex sRGB. See the colour
    section for why.
    
    This module imports nothing at all. Not Three, not your renderer, not a util file
    that imports Three three levels down. Check the actual import graph, not just the
    top of the file.
    
    ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    STAGE 2 — THE GEOMETRY COMPILER (the part that matters)
    
    One function:
    
      compileTerrain(grid, bounds) -> {
        positions: Float32Array,
        normals:   Float32Array,
        colors:    Float32Array,
        indices:   Uint32Array,
      }
    
    Rules:
    
    - No Three.js types anywhere in this file or anything it imports. Plain typed arrays
      in, plain typed arrays out.
    - Flat shading. Every face gets its own vertices with a face normal. Do not share
      vertices between faces. Shared vertices average the normals and turn crisp terrace
      edges into mush, which is exactly the look you are trying to avoid.
    - Preallocate growable buffers and reuse them across calls. This runs per tile, many
      times per second while the camera moves. Allocating fresh arrays each bake is the
      difference between smooth and stuttering.
    
    What to emit per cell:
    
    1. A top cap at y = level * LEVEL_HEIGHT.
    2. For each of the four neighbours whose level is LOWER (or which is outside the
       grid), a vertical side face spanning the height difference.
    
    Those side faces are the cliffs and they are most of what the player actually sees
    from a three-quarter camera. Get them correct and consistent before you add anything
    else. A terrain with perfect tops and wrong cliffs looks broken; the reverse looks
    stylised.
    
    Corner treatment: round every convex corner of the top cap with a small three-facet
    quarter-round instead of leaving it square. Write ONE helper that produces this arc
    and have every feature that follows the same corner call it — the cap, the cliff top,
    the water bank. If two features each approximate "the corner" separately they will
    drift by a fraction of a unit and you get a visible seam that is miserable to debug.
    
    ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    STAGE 3 — COLOUR (this is the whole look)
    
    Colour is per-vertex in the `colors` array. There are no textures anywhere.
    
    Write LINEAR RGB values. Three.js renders in a linear workflow and converts to sRGB
    at output. If you write sRGB values (i.e. what a hex colour picker gives you)
    straight into vertex colours, everything comes out washed and pale and you will spend
    a day blaming the lighting. Convert once at the material table: c^2.2, or use the
    proper piecewise transform.
    
    Per cell, mix its material colour along three signals before writing it:
    
      crest    — the bright pole, used at the top rim of a riser
      deep     — the dark pole, used at the foot of a riser and in shadowed pockets
      sediment — a third, differently-hued pole for ground cover variation
    
    Then, on the side faces:
    
      the whole face  = the material colour, darker and slightly DESATURATED
      the top ~15%    = a distinctly brighter rim band toward `crest`
    
    That rim band is the single highest-value thing in this entire brief. It is what
    makes the terrain read as drawn rather than as a lit polygon. Do not skip it and do
    not make it subtle.
    
    ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    STAGE 4 — CONTOURS
    
    Two ways to do this. Start with the first, understand the second.
    
    Simple version: emit separate LINE geometry along every silhouette edge — every edge
    where the level changes, plus the outer border. Render as its own object with a dark
    colour. Do NOT use a post-process outline pass: line geometry is cheaper, stays sharp
    at any zoom, and you decide exactly which edges get one, which a screen-space filter
    can never do.
    
    Grown-up version, which is what I ended up with: don't draw lines at all, darken the
    vertex colours in a band along those edges. Each mark class gets its own alpha and
    its own width in world units:
    
      wall contour     strong,  widest
      terrace contour  medium,  gated on a minimum drop so flat ground stays clean
      shoreline        medium,  gated on water CONTACT, since a waterline has no drop
      riser foot       weak,    a wide soft band pooling at the bottom of a cliff
    
    The foot band is the one people forget. A riser produces two visual events, a bright
    line at the top and gathered darkness at the bottom, and with only the top one the
    step looks pasted on.
    
    The trap: band width lives in world units but has to survive zooming out. A 4-unit
    band can land under 2 screen pixels at a wide framing, and a soft band under 2 pixels
    is indistinguishable from noise. Measure the delivered width in SCREEN pixels at your
    widest camera, not in the editor at your favourite zoom.
    
    Second trap, and this one cost me real time: if you decide band membership by
    distance from the tile contact point, your resolution is the tile lattice and every
    organic shoreline comes out visibly square. The geometry is fine, the pigment is
    what's blocky. Measure distance from the actual edge geometry.
    
    ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    STAGE 5 — WATER AND CHASMS
    
    Water: a separate translucent surface at a fixed inset BELOW the cell's stored level,
    so the bank always overlaps the water slightly. Coplanar surfaces are a z-fighting
    coin flip; the inset removes the whole class of bug. Where a water cell borders a
    lower neighbour, emit a waterfall quad down that cliff.
    
    Chasm: no top cap at all. The surrounding side faces extend downward, plus a dark
    floor far below. Give the floor a real, visibly lower position rather than a
    near-black plane just under the lip, otherwise it reads as a painted hole.

replies.author: idlerunner00
replies.body:
──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────  
STAGE 6 — THREADING  
  
\- Move the compiler into a Web Worker. Because it has no Three dependency this is a  
  file move, not a rewrite. That is the payoff for Stage 2's discipline.  
\- Return the typed arrays as TRANSFERABLES so nothing is copied.  
\- Split the world into tiles and bake at most one or two per frame. One large bake  
  stalls the frame visibly and users read it as a hitch, not as loading.  
\- Keep a pool of buffers and hand them back after upload. Per-bake allocation is a  
  GC sawtooth.  
\- Queue: latest-wins, keyed by tile plus generation. When a tile is invalidated while  
  a job for it is queued, the old job becomes a tombstone and is dropped at the root  
  rather than searched for. Camera movement invalidates faster than you can bake, so  
  a naive FIFO queue will spend its whole budget on stale work.  
  
──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────  
STAGE 7 — MATERIAL AND LIGHTING  
  
\- One material for the whole terrain, \`vertexColors: true\`. One draw call per tile,  
  never per cell.  
\- One directional light plus ambient. Keep the contrast LOW. The vertex colours are  
  carrying the image; the lighting only seats it in the scene. If you find yourself  
  tuning lights to fix the look, the fix belongs in the colour stage instead.  
\- If you write a custom shader, build the position with the full  
  projectionMatrix \* modelViewMatrix chain. Skipping modelMatrix silently opts that  
  object out of any world transform, and it will look correct until the first time  
  something rotates the world.  
  
──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────  
TESTS (write these as you go, not at the end)  
  
Against the compiler directly, no renderer, no canvas:  
  
  flat grid                    -> zero side faces  
  one raised cell              -> exactly four side faces  
  a 2-level step               -> side face height equals 2 \* LEVEL\_HEIGHT  
  water beside a drop          -> exactly one waterfall quad  
  every side face colour       -> darker than its own top face  
  every emitted triangle       -> counter-clockwise seen from outside  
  same grid compiled twice     -> byte-identical output  
  
That last one is worth more than it looks. Once you have it, hash the output of the  
worker path and the output of the synchronous path and assert they match. That single  
test is what stops the two paths from quietly becoming two different renderers.  
  
──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────  
PITFALLS I ALREADY HIT — do not rediscover these  
  
\- Never derive face winding from a projected screen area. A polygon that is nearly  
  edge-on to the camera has a screen area near zero and its SIGN is numerical noise,  
  so the face flips randomly as the camera moves. Resolve winding against the face's  
  own world-space normal.  
\- Never derive presence or visibility of a face from a camera-relative measure at  
  bake time. Bakes are cached and the camera is not.  
\- Reversed smoothstep (edge0 > edge1) is undefined in GLSL. It works on your GPU and  
  produces garbage on someone else's.  
\- \`half\` is a reserved word in GLSL. Using it as a variable name gives you a silently  
  black surface on some drivers, with no compile error you will ever see.  
\- Corner softening applied without a minimum-run gate turns a straight wall into  
  crenellations, because every cell corner gets rounded including the ones in the  
  middle of a flat run.  
\- Float32 has \~7 decimal digits. Do not put wall-clock milliseconds into a float32  
  attribute; at that magnitude one ulp is over a minute and your animation quantises  
  into visible jerks. Pass an epoch-relative offset instead.

replies.body: Say you have a bug where if you sell two items in a specific order they end up back in your inventory.  In a single player game that's on you for cheating, but in an MMO now you have ruined the economy for everyone.  You basically need end to end testing.  There's all sorts of different regulations for online content in different countries too.  Especially if your game is geared towards children.

replies.body: What does that have to do with three.js?

replies.author: idlerunner00
replies.body:
I just don't think any of them is a three.js problem. Three is a client-side renderer. That bug is a server authority and testing problem, and you'd have it identically with Babylon, PlayCanvas or raw WebGL.

Concretely in my case: three is a dependency of the client package only, the server doesn't import it and can't. The client never sends state, only intents, "I want to sell this". The sell logic lives in a shared domain layer that the server runs authoritatively. The client imports the same code for prediction and preview, so there's exactly one implementation of every rule, but the client's copy has no authority over anything.

replies.author: idlerunner00
replies.body:
I was gifted a GPT subscription, so I used both and tried to max them out. Generally I'd run one as the implementer and the other as a critic. Over time I got the impression that Claude is better at setting the foundation and GPT is better at finishing the visuals, so depending on the size of the task I'd have Claude break it down into up to 5 sessions that can run simultaneously, then hand the visual parts to Codex and the rest back to Claude. I tested all the available models but ended up mostly on Opus 4.8 (now 5), Fable and GPT 5.6 Sol.

I can't give you an honest number for time spent, because a lot of the concepts were written down long before this. The concept base was around 15 A4 pages, and on top of that every larger system has its own breakdown that I wrote before the first thing of that kind was being built, defining a subset of rules just for that area.

The test itself took about 6 weeks. I worked with loops and goals a lot, so many tasks ran very long. The longest single one ran for about 36 hours without a word from me.

That's the part I still find slightly insane, by the way: it can work that long unattended and still be doing something useful at the end. The 6 weeks were mostly me waiting. I'd draft task packages over the weekend, start a handful early in the morning or late in the evening, and look at the results later or the next day.
